# Thigh, knee, and popliteal fossa

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Rheumatology and immunology > Basics of rheumatology > Thigh, knee, and popliteal fossa*

[Original Article Link](/library/-o0DeS)

---

## Summary

The lower extremity consists of the hip, thigh, knee, <u>popliteal fossa</u>, <u>leg (crus), ankle, and foot</u>. The thigh is the portion of the lower limb extending from the hip to the knee. The knee is the <u>joint</u> that connects the thigh and the leg (crus). The space <u>posterior</u> to the knee is referred to as the <u>popliteal fossa</u>. The <u>femur</u> is the <u>long bone</u> of the thigh, which articulates proximally with the <u>acetabulum</u> of the <u>pelvis</u> to form the <u>hip joint</u> and distally with the tibial condyles and the patella to form <u>the knee joint</u>. The muscles of the thigh are separated by intermuscular septa into the <u>anterior</u>, <u>posterior</u>, and <u>medial</u> (adductor) compartments, all of which are enclosed by the <u>fascia</u> lata. The <u>anterior</u> compartment, which is innervated by the <u>femoral nerve</u>, contains muscles involved in knee extension and hip <u>flexion</u>. The <u>posterior</u> compartment (<u>hamstrings</u>), which is innervated by the tibial part of the <u>sciatic nerve</u>, contains muscles involved in hip extension and knee <u>flexion</u>. The <u>medial</u> (adductor) compartment, which is innervated by the <u>obturator nerve</u>, contains muscles involved in hip <u>adduction</u>, <u>flexion</u>, and <u>external rotation</u>. The <u>femoral triangle</u> is a triangular intermuscular space in the <u>anterior</u> thigh through which pass major neurovascular structures (<u>femoral artery</u>, <u>femoral vein</u>, <u>femoral nerve</u>). Additional noteworthy anatomic regions in the thigh include the <u>femoral canal</u>, <u>femoral ring</u>, and <u>adductor canal</u>. The thigh is <u>perfused</u> by the femoral and <u>obturator arteries</u> and drained by the <u>long saphenous vein</u> (<u>superficial</u>) and the <u>femoral vein</u> (deep). <u>The knee joint</u> consists of the tibiofemoral and patellofemoral <u>joints</u>. Soft-tissue structures of the knee include the <u>menisci</u> (<u>medial</u> and <u>lateral</u>), the cruciate <u>ligaments</u> (<u>anterior</u> and <u>posterior</u>), the collateral <u>ligaments</u> (<u>medial</u> and <u>lateral</u>), and the <u>bursae</u> (<u>prepatellar bursa</u>, <u>anserine bursa</u>). <u>The knee joint</u> allows for <u>flexion</u> and extension of the leg as well as a certain degree of <u>internal rotation</u> and <u>external rotation</u>. <u>The knee joint</u> is <u>perfused</u> by branches of the femoral and popliteal vessels and innervated by the genicular branches of the femoral, obturator, tibial, and common peroneal nerves. The <u>popliteal fossa</u> is a diamond-shaped region on the <u>posterior</u> aspect of the knee, which contains the <u>popliteal artery</u> and <u>vein</u> and the tibial and <u>common peroneal nerve</u>.

---

## The femur

### Overview




* The <u>femur</u> is the longest and strongest bone of the body.

* It articulates with:

* <u>Acetabulum</u> of the <u>pelvis</u> to form the <u>hip joint</u>

* Tibial condyles to form <u>the knee joint</u>





### Important landmarks




* Head

* A nearly spherical structure that articulates with the <u>acetabulum</u> of the <u>pelvis</u>.

* Has a notch, known as the fovea capitis, to which the round ligament of the hip is attached

* Vascular supply

* Branch of the <u>obturator artery</u> (travels through the <u>round ligament of the femur</u>)

* Arterial ring around the femoral neck: formed by the <u>medial</u> and <u>lateral femoral circumflex arteries</u>

* Clinical significance

* <u>Osteonecrosis of the femoral head</u>

* <u>Femoral head fracture</u>

* Neck

* Connects the head to the shaft of the <u>femur</u>

* Clinical significance: <u>femoral neck fracture</u>

* Greater trochanter: lies on the <u>lateral</u> aspect of the junction between the neck and shaft of the <u>femur</u>

* Lesser trochanter: lies on the posteromedial aspect of the junction between the neck and shaft of the <u>femur</u>

* Shaft

* Linea aspera: ridge seen on the <u>posterior</u> aspect of the shaft

* Pectineal line: <u>medial</u> border of the <u>linea aspera</u> to which the <u>pectineus muscle</u> is attached

* Adductor tubercle: a prominence above the <u>medial</u> femoral condyle to which the <u>adductor magnus muscle</u> is attached

* <u>Distal</u> end

* <u>Medial</u> and <u>lateral</u> condyles

* The inferior surface articulates with the tibial condyles to form <u>the knee joint</u>.

* The <u>anterior</u> surface articulates with the patella to form the patellofemoral <u>joint</u>.

* <u>Intercondylar fossa</u>: groove between the condyles to which the <u>anterior</u> and <u>posterior</u> cruciate <u>ligaments</u> are attached

## Muscles of the thigh

### Overview




The deep <u>fascia</u> of the thigh separates the muscles into three compartments:




* <u>Anterior</u> compartment

* Common nerve supply: <u>femoral nerve</u>

* Common function: knee extension

* <u>Posterior</u> compartment

* Common origin: the <u>ischial tuberosity</u>

* Common nerve supply: tibial part of the <u>sciatic nerve</u>

* Common function: hip extension and knee <u>flexion</u>

* <u>Medial</u> compartment

* Common nerve supply: <u>obturator nerve</u>

* Common function: hip <u>adduction</u>

## Femoral triangle and fasial compartments of the thigh

### Femoral triangle




* Definition: a triangular intermuscular space in the superomedial aspect of the <u>anterior</u> thigh through which the major neurovascular structures of the lower limb pass

* Boundaries

* Superior: <u>inguinal ligament</u>

* <u>Lateral</u>: <u>medial</u> border of the <u>sartorius</u>

* <u>Medial</u>: <u>medial</u> border of the <u>adductor longus</u>

* Floor: <u>adductor longus</u>, <u>iliopsoas</u>, and <u>pectineus</u> muscles

* Roof: <u>fascia</u> lata

* Contents (<u>lateral</u> to <u>medial</u>)

* <u>Femoral nerve</u>

* Femoral branch of the <u>genitofemoral nerve</u>

* <u>Femoral artery</u>

* <u>Femoral vein</u>

* <u>Femoral canal</u>

* <u>Lymphatics</u>

* Clinical significance

* Easy access into the arterial system via the <u>femoral artery</u> (e.g., <u>coronary angiography</u>)

* Easy access into the central venous system via the <u>femoral vein</u>

* <u>Femoral hernia</u>: <u>herniation</u> of intra-abdominal contents through the <u>femoral canal</u>





> [!NOTE]
> Venous close to <u>penis</u>. Nerves close to hip curves.




> [!NOTE]
> NAVEL: Nerve, Artery, Vein, Empty space (<u>femoral canal</u>), and Lymphatics (order of the <u>femoral triangle</u> contents, from <u>lateral</u> to <u>medial</u>).




![Femoral triangle and adductor canal](media/e2wkwi3npdl24z824z54r4ml.jpg)

Femoral triangle and adductor canal




#### Femoral canal




* Definition: a cylindrical space enclosed within the <u>femoral sheath</u> that contains loose areolar tissue and <u>lymphatics</u>

* Boundaries

* <u>Anterior</u>: <u>inguinal ligament</u>

* <u>Posterior</u>: pubic ramus and pectineal ligament

* <u>Medial</u>: lacunar ligament

* <u>Lateral</u>: <u>femoral vein</u>

* Clinical significance

* Accommodates venous dilation of the <u>femoral vein</u> in response to increased <u>venous return</u> from the lower limbs

* The <u>femoral canal</u> is wider in women, so women are more susceptible to developing <u>femoral hernias</u>.





![Femoral canal](media/gq95af1tgbzf4flpjq2srab4.jpg)

Femoral canal




#### Femoral sheath




* Definition: <u>connective tissue</u> formed by the iliac <u>fascia</u> and transversalis <u>fasciae</u> about 3–4 cm below the <u>inguinal ligament</u>

* Contents

* Encloses most contents of the <u>femoral triangle</u>, including:

* <u>Femoral vein</u>

* <u>Femoral artery</u>

* <u>Femoral canal</u>

* <u>Deep inguinal lymph nodes</u>

* Does not cover the <u>femoral nerve</u>

* Vertical septae divide the sheath into compartments for the contents of the <u>femoral triangle</u> (see above).





#### Femoral ring




* Definition: the abdominal opening of the <u>femoral canal</u>

* Boundaries

* <u>Anterior</u>: <u>inguinal ligament</u>

* <u>Posterior</u>: <u>pectineal ligament</u>

* <u>Medial</u>: <u>lacunar ligament</u>

* <u>Lateral</u>: <u>medial</u> border of the <u>femoral vein</u>





### Adductor canal




* Definition: a tunnel that extends from the apex of the <u>femoral triangle</u> to the adductor hiatus within the <u>adductor magnus</u>

* Boundaries

* <u>Anterior</u>: <u>sartorius</u>

* <u>Posterior</u>: <u>adductor magnus</u> and longus

* <u>Lateral</u>: <u>vastus medialis</u>

* Contents

* Femoral vessels

* <u>Saphenous nerve</u>

* Nerve to the <u>vastus medialis</u>

* Clinical significance: <u>Regional anesthesia</u> to the leg and <u>distal</u> thigh can be achieved by anesthetizing the <u>saphenous nerve</u> within the <u>adductor canal</u>.





### Saphenous opening




* Definition: an opening in the <u>fascia</u> lata of the thigh located 4 cm below and <u>lateral</u> to the pubic tubercle (a palpable bony prominence on the superior ramus of the <u>pubic bone</u>)

* Clinical significance: site of the <u>saphenofemoral junction</u>

* The <u>great saphenous vein</u> penetrates a <u>fascia</u> that covers the <u>saphenous opening</u> (known as the cribriform fascia) and drains into the <u>femoral vein</u>.

* For open <u>surgery</u> of <u>varicose veins</u>, a <u>skin</u> <u>incision</u> and main dissection are performed in this region.





![Saphenofemoral junction](media/oxdt4my7rdp57xq4p6gdkn6p.jpg)

## Vascular supply of the thigh

### <u>Arteries</u>




![Arteries of the lower extremity](media/id3mhivslblg69zzq1npew9j.jpg)

Arteries of the lower extremity

![Arteries of the lower extremity](media/yyh8uarjugriiiaz73lbcqcj.jpg)

Arteries of the lower extremity




#### Femoral artery




* Origin: continuation of the <u>external iliac artery</u>

* Course

* Begins behind the <u>inguinal ligament</u> at the midinguinal point

* Travels through the <u>femoral triangle</u> and the <u>adductor canal</u> (<u>anterior</u> thigh)

* Enters the <u>posterior compartment of the thigh</u> through the <u>adductor hiatus</u> where it continues as the <u>popliteal artery</u>

* Supplies: all compartments of the thigh





##### <u>Femoral artery</u> branches




* <u>Superficial</u> branches (superficial femoral artery): supply the <u>subcutaneous tissue</u> of the lower abdomen and <u>perineal region</u>

* <u>Superficial epigastric artery</u>

* <u>Superficial</u> circumflex <u>iliac artery</u>

* <u>Superficial</u> <u>external pudendal artery</u>

* Deep branches

* Profunda femoris artery

* Main branch of the <u>femoral artery</u> and the main <u>artery</u> of the thigh

* Named branches: <u>medial</u> and <u>lateral circumflex femoral arteries</u> that supply the head and neck of <u>femur</u> (see “<u>Osteonecrosis of the femoral head</u>”)

* Clinical significance: becomes the main collateral in <u>femoropopliteal disease</u>

* Deep <u>external pudendal artery</u>: supplies the <u>skin</u> of the <u>perineum</u>





![Arteries of the femoral head with watershed zone](media/ai2m020bw2c0tapygg2hcq1v.jpg)

Arteries of the femoral head with watershed zone




#### <u>Obturator artery</u>




* Origin: branch of the <u>internal iliac artery</u>

* Supplies: <u>medial compartment of the thigh</u>





### <u>Veins</u>




* <u>Superficial vein</u>: <u>long saphenous vein</u> (see “Vascular supply” in “<u>The leg, ankle, and foot</u>” article for more details)

* <u>Deep vein</u>: femoral vein

* Origin

* Continuation of the <u>popliteal vein</u>

* Begins at the <u>adductor hiatus</u> and accompanies the <u>femoral artery</u> throughout its course

* Becomes the <u>external iliac vein</u> behind the <u>inguinal ligament</u>

* Tributaries

* <u>Profunda femoris</u> <u>vein</u> (<u>deep vein</u> of the thigh)

* <u>Lateral</u> and <u>medial</u> circumflex <u>femoral veins</u>

## Innervation of the thigh

### Motor and sensory innervation




The motor and sensory nerve of the thigh arise from the lumbar plexus and sacral plexus.




| <br>Motor and sensory innervation of the thigh <br> |  |  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| <br>Nerves<br> |  | Origin | Motor supply | Sensory supply | Clinical significance |
| Mixed motor and sensory nerves | Femoral nerve | <br><br>* Largest branch of the <u>lumbar plexus</u><br><br>* <u>Nerve roots</u>: <u>dorsal</u> branches of L2–L4 <u>ventral rami</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* Muscles of the <u>anterior compartment of the thigh</u><br><br>* <u>Iliacus</u><br><br>* <u>Pectineus</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* Intermediate cutaneous nerve of thigh: <u>skin</u> over the <u>anterior</u> aspect of the thigh<br><br>* <u>Medial</u> cutaneous nerve of thigh (<u>medial</u> femoral cutaneous nerve): <u>skin</u> over the lower 2/3<sup>rd</sup> of the <u>medial</u> aspect of the thigh<br><br>* <u>Saphenous nerve</u>: supplies the <u>medial</u> side of the leg and foot<br><br>* Articular branch: <u>knee joint</u><br><br><br> | <br>* <u>Femoral nerve injury</u><br><br> |
| Obturator nerve | <br><br>* Branch of the <u>lumbar plexus</u><br><br>* <u>Nerve roots</u>: <u>ventral</u> branches of L2–L4 <u>ventral rami</u><br><br><br> | <br>* Muscles of the <u>medial compartment of the thigh</u><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Skin</u> over the upper 1/3<sup>rd</sup> of the <u>medial</u> aspect of the thigh<br><br>* Articular branch: hip and <u>knee joints</u><br><br><br> | <br>* <u>Obturator nerve injury</u><br><br> |  |
| Sciatic nerve | <br><br>* <u>Sacral plexus</u><br><br>* <u>Nerve roots</u>: L4–<u>S3</u><br><br>* Enters the <u>posterior</u> thigh through the <u>greater sciatic foramen</u><br><br>* Thickest nerve of the body<br><br><br> | <br>* Tibial part of <u>sciatic nerve</u><br><br>* Muscles of the <u>posterior compartment of the thigh</u> (<u>hamstrings</u>)<br><br>* Hamstring portion of the <u>adductor magnus</u><br><br>* Terminal branches: divides usually at the apex of the <u>popliteal fossa</u> into the <u>tibial nerve</u> and common fibular nerves that supply the leg and foot<br><br> | <br>* None in the thigh (see “Innervation” in “<u>The leg, ankle, and foot</u>” article for further detail)<br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Sciatica</u><br><br>* <u>Sciatic nerve injury</u><br><br><br> |  |
| Pure sensory nerves | <br>Lateral cutaneous nerve of thigh (lateral femoral cutaneous nerve) | <br>* <u>Lumbar plexus</u> (L2–L3)<br><br> | <br>* None<br><br> | <br>* <u>Skin</u> over the anterolateral aspect of the thigh (up to the knee)<br><br> | <br>* <u>Meralgia paresthetica</u><br><br> |
| <br>Posterior cutaneous nerve of thigh (<u>posterior femoral cutaneous nerve</u>) | <br>* <u>Sacral plexus</u> (<u>S2</u>–<u>S3</u>)<br><br> | <br>* None<br><br> | <br>* <u>Skin</u> over the buttock, <u>posterior</u> part of the <u>perineum</u>, and <u>posterior</u> thigh<br><br> | <br>* <u>Posterior</u> thigh and <u>pelvic pain</u> [[2]](/library/FKXgR_)<br><br> |  |

### <u>Dermatomal</u> distribution of the thigh and knee




* <u>Anterior</u> thigh (craniocaudal): L2–L4

* <u>Posterior</u> thigh (lateromedial and caudocranial): <u>S1</u>–<u>S4</u>

* <u>Anterior</u> knee: L3, L4

* <u>Popliteal fossa</u>: <u>S1</u>, <u>S2</u>

## The knee joint

### Overview




* Type of <u>joint</u>: a complex hinge type of <u>synovial joint</u> made up of two components

* The tibiofemoral articulation

* Between the condyles of the <u>tibia</u> and <u>femur</u>

* <u>Weight-bearing</u>

* The patellofemoral articulation

* Between the <u>anterior</u> surface of the femoral condyles and the <u>posterior</u> surface of the patella

* Not <u>weight-bearing</u>

* Movements

* <u>Flexion</u>: <u>hamstrings</u>, <u>sartorius</u>, <u>gracilis</u>, <u>popliteus</u>

* Extension: <u>quadriceps femoris</u>

* <u>External rotation</u> of the flexed knee: <u>biceps femoris</u> and <u>sartorius</u>

* <u>Internal rotation</u> of the flexed knee: <u>semimembranosus</u>, <u>semitendinosus</u>, <u>gracilis</u>

* Blood supply: <u>anastomosis</u> around <u>the knee joint</u> between branches of the femoral and popliteal vessels (genicular <u>anastomosis</u>)

* Innervation: genicular branches of the femoral, obturator, tibial, and common peroneal nerves





### <u>Soft tissue</u> structures of the knee




#### <u>Ligaments</u> and <u>menisci</u>




| <u>Ligaments</u> and <u>menisci</u> of the knee |  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Structure |  | Anatomy | Function | Testing |
| Cruciate <u>ligaments</u> | <br>Anterior cruciate ligament (<u>ACL</u>) | <br><br>* Origin: <u>anterior</u> intercondylar part of the <u>tibia</u><br><br>* Insertion: <u>lateral</u> femoral condyle (posteromedial aspect)<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Prevents <u>anterior</u> displacement of the <u>tibia</u> on the <u>femur</u><br><br>* Limits hyperextension of the knee<br><br>* Clinical significance: <u>ACL injury</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Lachman test</u><br><br>* <u>Anterior drawer test</u><br><br>* <u>Pivot shift test</u><br><br><br> |
| <br>Posterior cruciate ligament (<u>PCL</u>) | <br><br>* Origin: <u>posterior</u> intercondylar part of the <u>tibia</u><br><br>* Insertion: <u>medial</u> femoral condyle (<u>lateral</u> aspect)<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Prevents <u>posterior</u> displacement of the <u>tibia</u> on the <u>femur</u><br><br>* Limits hyperflexion of the knee<br><br>* Is thicker and less liable to injury than the <u>ACL</u><br><br>* Clinical significance: <u>PCL injury</u> (<u>dashboard injury</u>)<br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Posterior drawer test</u><br><br>* <u>Quadriceps active test</u><br><br><br> |  |
| Collateral <u>ligaments</u> | <br>Medial collateral ligament (<u>tibial collateral ligament</u>; <u>MCL</u>) | <br><br>* Origin: <u>medial</u> femoral epicondyle<br><br>* Insertion: <u>medial</u> tibial condyle<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Prevents <u>medial</u> displacement of the <u>tibia</u> and <u>femur</u> (valgus)<br><br>* Limits <u>abduction</u> of the leg at <u>the knee joint</u><br><br><br> | <br>* <u>Valgus stress test</u><br><br> |
| <br>Lateral collateral ligament (<u>fibular collateral ligament</u>; <u>LCL</u>) | <br><br>* Origin: <u>lateral</u> femoral epicondyle<br><br>* Insertion: head of the <u>fibula</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* Prevents <u>lateral</u> displacement of the <u>tibia</u> and <u>femur</u> (varus)<br><br>* Limits extension and <u>adduction</u> of the leg at <u>the knee joint</u><br><br><br> | <br>* <u>Varus stress test</u><br><br> |  |
| <br><br>Other <u>ligaments</u> of the knee<br> | <br>Patellar ligament (<u>patellar tendon</u>) | <br><br>* The continuation of the <u>quadriceps femoris</u> <u>tendon</u><br><br>* Insertion: <u>Tibial tuberosity</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* Keeps the patella in place<br><br>* Biomechanical function in walking and running<br><br>* Clinical significance<br><br>* <u>Patellar tendinitis</u><br><br>* <u>Patellar tendon tear</u><br><br><br> | <br>* Extension of the knee<br><br> |
| Popliteofibular ligament | <br><br>* Origin: <u>popliteus</u> <u>tendon</u><br><br>* Insertion: head of <u>fibula</u><br><br><br> | <br>* Stabilizes the posterolateral aspect of the knee<br><br> | <br><br>* Cannot be tested in isolation<br><br>* <u>Varus stress test</u><br><br><br> |  |
| Transverse <u>ligament</u> | <br>* Connects the <u>anterior</u> ends of the two <u>menisci</u><br><br> | <br><br>* Prevents the <u>anterior</u> margin (horn) of the <u>menisci</u> from moving forward<br><br>* Reduces the pressure exerted on the <u>menisci</u> by the articular surfaces of the <u>tibia</u> and <u>femur</u><br><br><br> | <br>* Cannot be tested in isolation<br><br> |  |
| Anterolateral ligament | <br><br>* Origin: <u>lateral</u> femoral epicondyle<br><br>* Insertion: <u>proximal</u> <u>tibia</u> (anterolateral aspect)<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Stabilization during <u>internal rotation</u> at <u>flexion</u> angles ≥ 35°<br><br>* May stabilize internal tibial rotation [[3]](/library/HV1KDf0)<br><br><br> | <br>* Cannot be tested in isolation<br><br> |  |
| <br><u>Menisci</u><br>(semilunar cartilages) | Medial meniscus | <br><br>* C-shaped fibrous <u>cartilage</u> on the <u>medial</u> condylar surface of the <u>tibia</u><br><br>* Attached to the <u>tibial collateral ligament</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* Deepen the articular surface and stabilize <u>the knee joint</u> structure<br><br>* Decrease friction between the osseous surfaces<br><br>* Periphery is better vascularized than the inner surface<br><br>* Clinical significance: <u>meniscal tear</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>McMurray test</u><br><br>* <u>Apley grind test</u><br><br>* <u>Thessaly test</u><br><br><br> |
| Lateral meniscus | <br><br>* Circular fibrous <u>cartilage</u> on the <u>lateral</u> condylar surface of the <u>tibia</u><br><br>* Separated from the <u>fibular collateral ligament</u> by the <u>tendon</u> of the <u>popliteus</u><br><br><br> |  |  |  |





> [!NOTE]
> The <u>unhappy triad</u>: injury to the <u>ACL</u>, <u>MCL</u>, and <u>medial meniscus</u> caused by a <u>lateral</u> force to the knee.




> [!NOTE]
> To remember the orientation of the cruciate <u>ligaments</u>, cross your middle finger over the index finger of the same hand and hold your hand over the <u>ipsilateral</u> knee. The middle finger represents the <u>ACL</u> (from <u>lateral</u> femoral condyle to <u>anterior</u> <u>tibia</u>) and the index finger represents the <u>PCL</u> (from <u>medial</u> femoral condyle to <u>posterior</u> <u>tibia</u>).

| <u>Bursae</u> of the knee |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
| <u>Bursae</u> | Anatomy | Clinical significance |
| Suprapatellar bursa | <br><br>* Deep to the <u>quadriceps femoris muscle</u><br><br>* Communicates with <u>the knee joint</u> cavity<br><br><br> | <br>* Suprapatellar <u>bursitis</u><br><br> |
| Prepatellar bursa | <br>* Between the <u>anterior</u> surface of the patella and the <u>skin</u><br><br> | <br>* <u>Prepatellar bursitis</u> (<u>housemaid's knee</u>)<br><br> |
| Infrapatellar bursa | <br><br>* Deep <u>infrapatellar bursa</u>: between the <u>tibia</u> and the <u>patellar ligament</u><br><br>* Subcutaneous <u>infrapatellar bursa</u>: between the <u>tibial tuberosity</u> and <u>skin</u><br><br><br> | <br>* Infrapatellar <u>bursitis</u> (clergyman's knee)<br><br> |
| Anserine bursa | <br>* Between the <u>tibial collateral ligament</u> and the <u>tendons</u> of <u>gracilis</u>, <u>semitendinosus</u>, and <u>sartorius</u> muscles (<u>medial</u> aspect of the knee)<br><br> | <br>* <u>Pes anserine bursitis</u><br><br> |

## The popliteal fossa

* Definition: a diamond-shaped region on the <u>posterior</u> aspect of the knee through which neurovascular structures pass from the thigh to the leg or vice versa

* Boundaries

* Superomedial: <u>semimembranosus</u> and <u>semitendinosus</u> muscles

* Superolateral: <u>biceps femoris</u> muscle

* Inferomedial: <u>medial</u> head of the <u>gastrocnemius</u> muscle

* Inferolateral: <u>lateral</u> head of the <u>gastrocnemius</u> muscle

* Floor

* <u>Posterior</u> aspect of <u>the knee joint</u> and <u>distal</u> <u>femur</u>

* Popliteus muscle

* Origin: <u>lateral</u> femoral condyle

* Insertion: posteriomedial surface of the <u>proximal</u> <u>tibia</u>, just below the <u>medial</u> tibial condyle

* Innervation: <u>tibial nerve</u>

* Action: <u>internally rotates</u> the <u>tibia</u> on the <u>femur</u>

* Roof: deep <u>fascia</u> and <u>skin</u>

* Contents (from <u>superficial</u> to deep)

* Nerves: <u>tibial nerve</u> and <u>common peroneal nerve</u> (see “<u>The leg, ankle, and foot</u>” for more details)

* <u>Vein</u>: popliteal vein

* Origin: formed by the union of <u>anterior</u> tibial, <u>posterior</u> tibial, and the <u>fibular veins</u> at the inferior border of the <u>popliteus</u>

* Becomes the <u>femoral vein</u> at the <u>adductor hiatus</u>

* Main tributary: <u>short saphenous vein</u>

* <u>Artery</u>: popliteal artery

* Origin

* Continuation of the <u>femoral artery</u>

* Begins at the <u>adductor hiatus</u>

* Ends at the inferior border of the <u>popliteus</u> by dividing into the <u>anterior tibial artery</u> and the tibioperoneal trunk

* Branches

* Genicular branches supply the <u>anastomosis</u> around <u>the knee joint</u>

* Muscular branches to the surrounding muscles

* Clinical significance

* <u>Popliteal cyst</u> (<u>Baker cyst</u>)

* <u>Popliteal artery aneurysm</u>





References:[[5]](/library/ES08Yf)
